description: Welcome! Our team is tackling the "Planet X and SPHEREx" challenge. We aim to combine space data analysis with an intuitive UI and a strong presentation. We are open to team members of all skill levels, especially developers, designers, and researchers. Join us and let's explore the cosmos together!
summary:
While NASA’s SPHEREx mission makes an unprecedented 102-band infrared all-sky map publicly available, the data itself remains trapped in raw, complex FITS files and astrometric catalogs. For a student or aspiring amateur, opening a raw spectrum to identify water ice absorption lines or performing epoch-to-epoch image subtraction to spot a fast-moving brown dwarf requires specialized Python pipelines, deep domain knowledge, and mastery of legacy academic archives like IRSA.
In Kazakhstan, a nation of over 20 million people with fewer than 50 professional astrophysicists and almost no local astronomy club infrastructure—this technical wall completely isolates curious youth from real observational science. Open data is technically "free," yet practically inaccessible without mentorship or native-language guidance.
details:
SPHEREx Chronos is an interactive, browser-based 3D website designed to make complex NASA space telescope data easy for anyone to explore and understand. While the SPHEREx mission shares an incredible 102-band infrared map of the sky with the public, that data is stored in raw scientific files and tables that normally require advanced coding skills and special software to read. Our platform acts as a simple visual bridge: when a user clicks on a space object—like the variable star R Draconis or the cold brown dwarf WISE 0855—our Python and FastAPI backend uses Astropy and NumPy to pull real data from SPHEREx, Gaia DR3, and WISE. In seconds, the app draws 102-channel infrared light graphs that show what the object is made of, such as water ice, carbon dioxide, and methane. It also uses Image Subtraction to compare space photos taken in different years, hiding stationary background stars so users can clearly see moving objects travel across the sky. On the screen, Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Three.js turn these real coordinates into a smooth 3D space map that works on regular student laptops with no downloads needed.

The main goal of SPHEREx Chronos is to remove the technical and language barriers that keep students and beginners away from real space research. Most professional astronomy tools are hard to use and exist only in English, leaving non-English speakers without easy access to modern science. By offering full localization in Kazakh, Russian, and English, we make NASA’s discoveries accessible in users' native languages. What makes our project truly creative is our "Double-Click AI Mentor": instead of forcing beginners to read long, boring textbooks, a built-in AI helper looks at the exact star or graph on the screen and explains difficult terms—like light absorption or star movement—in simple, everyday words whenever the user clicks on them. When building the app, our team focused on fast performance on basic computers, real scientific accuracy, and clear native-language learning, creating a tool that turns curious students into active citizen scientists right from their web browsers.
